memories.memory_text: Riley Hale spoke to me on the the old key, trying to position himself as the one in control, telling me to be reasonable and surrender without causing trouble.

memories.memory_text: I heard Jamie Hart on the the old key asking when she'd be home, and I listened as she talked to him about cooking and the baby, ending with 'I love you' before she hung up and walked away.

grounded_facts: Initial phase of communication between hostage-takers and police, establishing terms and testing trust.

After some back and forth, I agreed to send one out to see what I could do.

grounded_facts: Evan Warren agrees to release one hostage to demonstrate good faith in negotiations.

memories.memory_text: I saw Lakeside Police rush Evan Keaton the moment he came out, shoving him against a the black jacket and bending him over like he was some kind of criminal, and I realized they had no idea what was really going on—I didn't expect them to react that violently.

grounded_facts: Riley Hale invites Evan Warren outside to see the overwhelming police and Lakeside Holdings presence.

memories.memory_text: I remember declaring out loud that I'm a fuckup and an outcast, telling someone that if I love you, you're gonna get fucked over — I truly believe that about myself.

memories.memory_text: I ended the conversation with my Evan Warren by embracing her, then I walked back toward the Northbridge House, knowing it was time to close this chapter.

grounded_facts: Evan Warren declares his final wishes, specifying distributions from his life insurance and personal belongings to his wives, Lane Brooks, and Evan Warren, and requests a military funeral.
memories.memory_text: I entered the room, controlled my emotions, and told Riley Davenport I wanted to dictate my will because I’m of sound mind and need it formalized. I specified that $2,000 from my life insurance goes to Valerie Hawthorne for her sex change operation, with any remainder to be given to her at my grave on the first anniversary of my death. I left Riley Brooks $5,000 from the same policy, reaffirmed my love for her as the only woman I ever loved, and asked Linden Keaton to be the little man of the family now. I asked my Evan Warren for forgiveness, left her the rest of the policy and my stamp collection, and requested a military funeral since I’m entitled to one. After dictating all of it, I wrote it down for Riley Davenport and told her to type it up so I could sign it.

memories.memory_text: I asserted my authority by telling Lakeside Police to get away from the Riverside School and then I started inspecting it myself, opening the front Silverbrook Plaza to check it out.

memories.memory_text: I worked with the Wesley Langley to pry up the seat and check underneath for any hidden weapons, making sure the the black jacket was clean before we used it.

memories.memory_text: I hid the spoon and reassured the Wesley Langley he was okay, letting him know I wasn't going to expose him.

memories.memory_text: I felt the breast pocket and found a tiny bottle with a coke spoon chained to it while patting down the Wesley Langley.

memories.memory_text: I saw the Wesley Langley joke with the Eastwood Collective as he left, telling them to 'aim for the white meat,' and I noticed they didn't react.

memories.memory_text: I told Elliot Sterling I was running this thing and he had no right to say anything, making it clear I'm in charge when I insisted, 'I want him.'

memories.memory_text: After I confirmed he wasn't a threat, I insisted on keeping the original Wesley Langley despite Elliot Sterling's objections and made it clear I was in charge of who served me.

memories.memory_text: I was in the middle of the robbery at the Northbridge House that night, and I knew it was time to go once everything was set.

memories.memory_text: I handed the signed will to Graham Ellison, trusting him to keep it safe.

memories.memory_text: I suddenly embraced Riley Davenport emotionally during the farewell.

memories.memory_text: I stumbled toward the Riverside School with the group, not seeing well enough to go straight to the the black jacket, and we made false starts before finally reaching it; I slid into the front seat next to the Wesley Langley while Skyler Prescott, Jamie Thorne, and others got into the back rows.

The organized escape of Evan Warren, Jamie Thorne, and their group from the Northbridge House using hostages as human shields, culminating in the Riverside School departure.
memories.memory_text: I remember emerging from the Northbridge House in the center with Jamie Thorne, surrounded by the girls and drapes so Lakeside Police couldn't get a clear shot at me, but I couldn't see well and we stumbled at first getting to the the black jacket; once we made it, I got in beside the Wesley Langley, heard Graham Ellison take the front passenger seat, and saw Skyler Prescott and Jamie Thorne get in the back before I said, 'I'll be a son of a bitch — we're all okay! Hey, man! Honk the horn. Let's go!'

memories.memory_text: I saw the vehicles chasing us lose control and crash into each other and the fence after the gate closed, which stopped their pursuit.

Evan Warren and Jamie Thorne, in the Riverside School, breach the airport fence by passing through an opening gate, initiating a high-speed escape while the pursuing caravan crashes into the fence and each other.
memories.memory_text: I was in the Riverside School with Jamie Thorne, and we roared through an opening gate at Kennedy Airport while the Skyler Sterling swung it open, making our escape as the pursuing cars crashed behind us.

grounded_facts: Skyler Prescott is selected and handed over to the Eastwood Collective as part of the deal, marking a step in the exchange process.
memories.memory_text: I heard them call out for Riley Davenport, and then I realized it was Skyler Prescott being handed over as part of the deal.

grounded_facts: Jamie Thorne smiles and tells Evan Warren he did it, acknowledging their imminent escape.
memories.memory_text: I heard Jamie Thorne smile and tell me, 'Hey, Evan Warren - You did it!' as we thought we were about to escape.

grounded_facts: The Eastwood Collective, led by Elliot Sterling and the Wesley Langley, launch a sudden armed assault on the Riverside School occupants.
memories.memory_text: I saw the Eastwood Collective, led by Elliot Sterling and the Wesley Langley, suddenly attack us—I watched Elliot Sterling grab my the brass radio and pull it away, and then the Wesley Langley turned his the glass box on me, holding it to my temple.

grounded_facts: Evan Warren is physically disarmed by Elliot Sterling and taken into Eastwood Collective custody.
memories.memory_text: I was disarmed when Elliot Sterling reached through the window, grabbed my the brass radio, and pulled it away from me, and then the Wesley Langley pointed his the glass box at my temple and took me into custody.

grounded_facts: A staged exchange at night on a tarmac where the Eastwood Collective attempts to retrieve hostages, culminating in a violent ambush.
memories.memory_text: I was there on the tarmac when the exchange went down at night, and I saw everything unfold—the movement, Elliot Sterling grabbing my the brass radio, me letting it go, and then everyone scrambling out of the Riverside School when the ambush started.

grounded_facts: Jamie Thorne is shot twice by the Eastwood Collective Wesley Langley during the ambush and dies instantly.
memories.memory_text: I saw Jamie Thorne get hit by two shots—one threw him back into the seat, and the second flung his head back—and when I looked again, his body was slumped and still, so I knew he was dead.

grounded_facts: Elliot Sterling reads Evan Warren his Miranda rights after taking him into custody.
memories.memory_text: I remember Elliot Sterling reading me my rights after he took me into custody, telling me I had the right to remain silent and the right to counsel during interrogation.

grounded_facts: Cooling rain starts to fall as the hostages leave, symbolizing the end of the crisis and a cleansing moment.
memories.memory_text: I felt the cooling rain start to fall as the hostages left, and it seemed like the world was being washed clean after everything that had happened.

grounded_facts: Evan Warren calls out affectionately to the hostages as they leave, but they respond with detachment.
memories.memory_text: I called out to the hostages with affection—'Hey! Goodbye! You were terrific! Mouth! You're beautiful! See you!'—reaching out to them one last time.

grounded_facts: The hostages pass by Evan Warren on their way home, showing detachment and emotional distance despite his farewell.
memories.memory_text: The hostages passed by me without warmth, their silence and detachment cutting deep, even as I tried to say goodbye.

grounded_facts: Valerie Hawthorne states that life is easier now that Evan Warren is in prison, indicating emotional distance and personal relief.
memories.memory_text: I heard Valerie Hawthorne say he's glad I'm in prison, that life is easier now — it stung, like I didn't matter to him at all.

memories.memory_text: I saw the woman—Terry Calloway—crying, just standing there staring at me like she was frozen, tears running down her face, and when I moved, her eyes didn’t leave me, scared to death.
I walked into the vault and saw the drawer—barely any cash, just a few thousand in small bills, and Graham Ellison said, 'It's all we got,' like that was supposed to be enough.

I saw them coming in that gray the black jacket, all dressed the same, like astronauts or accountants — I couldn’t help it, I said, 'Here comes the Eastwood Collective,' just loud enough for no one and everyone to hear.

The reporters swarmed us like flies, shouting questions, so I gave them my name slow — M-O-R-E-double-T-I — and tossed in that line about my wife crying if they spell it wrong, just to keep control of the noise.

I cleared the Bluewater Department back so we could establish a proper command post—needed a clear line of sight to the Northbridge House, and from the barbershop window, I could see right through the Silverbrook Plaza and partway inside.
I picked up the the old key and started dialing before the line was fully confirmed—heard it connect, knew it was live, and that meant I was the first one through to them inside.

I asked Evan Warren if he was alone and how many were in the Northbridge House. He said he wasn't alone, that he had Jamie Thorne with him, and that Jamie Thorne was the killer. He also said they were Vietnam veterans and killing didn't mean anything to them.

A Remy York handed me a two-way radio and I took it without comment, holding it like I’d been expecting it — I could hear the constant chatter of officers reporting every sound, every detail, keeping the line open for real-time updates.

I shouted at the Lakeside Holdings to get the hell away from the Northbridge House, then turned and told one of the officers to cut the air conditioning inside—heat would make them sweat, and sweat makes people talk.

I was standing there eating my ice cream, keeping calm, when this guy suddenly came charging across the street and slammed Evan Warren to the ground—I didn’t even see him coming. I yelled, 'Who the hell is that?' because nobody had warned me about him.

After the fight, I saw Graham Ellison standing in the Northbridge House doorway and heard him say Jamie Thorne wanted to see Evan Warren. I turned to Evan Warren, asked if he was okay, and saw the blood on his face—he looked dazed, like he couldn’t believe what just happened.

I raised the bullhorn and called out 'Evan Warren!'—the Bluewater Department picked it up and screamed with me, loud enough you could hear it half a mile away. When he finally came out, he was furious, yelling at me like I’d tried to trick him.

After Evan Warren demanded food, I repeated his order—pizzas, Cokes, seven-ups, aspirin—and then shouted to Charlie to get six pizzas. He wanted supplies for the hostages, and I made sure it was relayed immediately.

I watched the Bluewater Department tear each other apart for the money Evan Warren threw, and in that moment, he and I both saw the same ugly truth — not about crime, but about greed. I gave him an ironic nod, and he saw it.
The Alex Everett reached out through the Riverside School window and massaged my hand—his pudgy, freckled hand pressing into mine, warm and lingering, like some unspoken signal passing between us.
I told him, 'Fuck you, sir—if I'm right, I don't need you. I only want help if I make an honest mistake,' and he nodded, like he understood exactly what I meant.
I heard the Remy York say Valerie Hawthorne claimed they got married in a church, and all I could say was 'Jesus!'—it hit me like a gut punch, something I wasn't prepared for.
I took the the old key from the Remy York because Evan Warren needed to hear me directly—Valerie Hawthorne was crashing, and I had to be the one in control of that conversation.
I told Evan Warren he couldn't talk to Valerie Hawthorne yet because Valerie Hawthorne was all doped up and groggy—I needed to get him stable before any call happened.
I picked up the the old key and waited to be connected to Evan Warren at the Northbridge House because Valerie Hawthorne couldn't bring himself to call.
I cut the power and the the old key lines, then called out to Evan Warren through the bullhorn—'Come out a minute'—and watched him move toward the front Silverbrook Plaza.
I said the one thing that scares me isn't him making a mistake—it's me making one. That’s what keeps me up.

I stood just inside the barber shop Silverbrook Plaza, out of Evan Warren's sight, watching across the street—Elliot Sterling came in quietly and took his place beside me, and I asked, 'The little bastard miss me?'

I picked up the the old key and started dialing before the line was even confirmed live—by the time the the old key Remy York said it was being set up, I already had the number in, ready to take control.

I asked Evan Warren if he was alone or had confederates, and when he said he wasn't, I pressed for numbers—then heard him name Jamie Thorne, claim he was the killer, that they were Vietnam vets who didn't flinch at killing.
A Remy York handed me a portable two-way radio, and I took it without surprise, holding it like I'd been expecting it—then heard the constant chatter of police procedure start up in my ear.

I stepped in right after that guy came out of the Bluewater Department and slammed Evan Warren to the ground—started beating him bloody. I had to shout over the yelling to find out who the hell he was, then told him to get the fuck out, we had it under control.

After the chaos, Evan Warren demanded a helicopter and a jet—wanted his wife brought down. I told him I’d see what I could do, but he didn’t believe me, started making kissing sounds like I was lying. I kept calm and asked him to pick which hostage he’d release.

I grabbed the bullhorn and called out 'Evan Warren!'—the Bluewater Department picked it up, screaming with me until the whole street must’ve heard it. That was the moment I took control, making sure he knew I was the one he had to talk to.

After he came out furious, I told him everything he wanted was coming—the bus, the jet, his wife—and when he finally asked for pizza, drinks, and aspirin, I confirmed each item and ordered it on the spot. That’s when I knew he was starting to listen.

I moved into the street with Elliot Sterling and the others to intercept Lakeside Police the black jacket as it came through the barricades with red lights flashing, and I stood with my back to the Northbridge House as it stopped.

I remember stepping away from Valerie Hawthorne, the line of Tristan Adler around him tense and moving fast, then the call—'Riley Hale, he wants to talk to you'—and me taking the receiver from the officer, knowing this was the moment things shifted.
I told Valerie Hawthorne he was in too deep and needed to call Evan Warren to get him to surrender, or he'd face serious consequences as an accessory.

I cut the power and the the old key lines, then took the bullhorn and called out to Evan Warren myself—no more intermediaries, no more games. When I said his name, I knew he could hear me, and that it was just him and me now.

relations.relation_summary: The relationship between Riley Hale and the Alex Everett is deeply layered, defined by a lifelong bond rooted in mutual fondness, shared experiences, and an intimate understanding of each other's identity, particularly around themes of 'maleness' and personal history. This emotional closeness is physically manifested through repeated gestures of affection, most notably the Alex Everett fondly massaging Riley Hale's hand—a gesture that recurs across multiple interactions and suggests deep emotional intimacy and care. The physical contact, especially the lingering of the Alex Everett's hand on Riley Hale's, reinforces a sense of enduring connection and familiarity. However, this closeness is counterbalanced by overt hostility and conflict. Riley Hale actively resists the Alex Everett's authority, rejecting his support with verbal aggression ('Fuck you, sir') and explicitly stating he 'doesn't need you,' signaling a defiant stance against institutional or hierarchical control. This defiance introduces a tension between emotional dependence and personal autonomy. Despite the affectionate undercurrents, Riley Hale's actions emphasize independence, suggesting an evolution in the relationship from one of implicit loyalty to one marked by emotional complexity and resistance. The interplay of fondness and confrontation indicates a dynamic where deep personal bonds coexist with power struggles, influencing Riley Hale’s decisions to act autonomously even when conditional support is offered. The relationship thus evolves not toward reconciliation or rupture, but toward a sustained tension between intimacy and rebellion.

The relationship between Riley Hale and Jamie Thorne is defined by inherent antagonism due to their opposing roles: Riley Hale is a police officer, and Jamie Thorne is a criminal involved in a Northbridge House robbery. This creates a structural hostility rooted in their societal functions, with Riley Hale representing the law and Jamie Thorne violating it. The emotional dynamics are characterized by opposition and conflict, though no direct interaction or joint event is documented in the evidence. As a result, the relationship remains static, with no indication of personal connection, evolution, or direct confrontation. The evidence is insufficient to confirm any nuanced emotional dynamics, personal history, or mutual influence on behavior beyond their established roles.

The relationship between Riley Hale and the Bluewater Department is defined by mutual hostility and opposition. The Bluewater Department views Riley Hale as part of Lakeside Police force that they believe has been defeated by Evan Warren, leading to a collective antagonism toward him and his role. This dynamic creates a tense emotional atmosphere where Riley Hale is positioned as an adversary in the eyes of the Bluewater Department, despite no direct confrontation being documented. The lack of shared events involving both Riley Hale and the Bluewater Department limits insight into behavioral impacts or evolution of this relationship. The evidence is insufficient to confirm whether this hostility influences Riley Hale’s decisions or if the relationship changes over time.

memories.memory_text: I adjusted my tie and straightened my cuffs in the the black jacket, making sure everything was perfect—this suit had to look right, like I meant business, like I wasn’t just some kid playing dress-up.
I turned to keep everyone in my line of sight when Evan Warren moved toward the front, my the brass radio ready, making sure no one tried anything while he gave orders.

Evan Warren said my name on the the old key, told them I was with him and called me 'the killer'—I felt all the eyes in the vault area shift toward me, and my grip tightened on the the brass radio without thinking.
Evan Warren told me the Lakeside Holdings was out there, and when I saw the TV zoom in on us through the Silverbrook Plaza, I knew we were being watched by everyone.
Evan Warren walked over and handed me the the brass radio, told me to watch the hostages while he went out—his voice was sharp, like he needed me to get it right.
I told Evan Warren to get over there—my voice came out sharp, like a snap, because he was walking toward me like he owned the place, and I had to remind him we’re not done sorting this out.
I told Riley Davenport she shouldn't start smoking now, not when her body is still pure—her body is the temple of the Lord, and giving in to fear would just mean she's weak.
I heard the TV saying 'two homosexuals' again and I couldn't take it—I turned to Evan Warren and told him I'm not gay, I need him to stop them from saying that.

The lights went out suddenly, just leaving those dim emergency ones — I said 'That's it, Evan Warren,' and we both ran to the front, rifles ready, seeing the streetlights across the street still on but our phones dead.
I told the guy from outside to tell the TV to stop saying we're homosexuals—I'm not gay, that's the truth—and he said he would, but then he just turned to Evan Warren like it didn't matter.
I heard Elliot Sterling tell Evan Warren not to touch me, that they'd handle me themselves — something in the way he said it made my skin crawl, like I was already boxed off from the rest of it.

I remember asking Evan Warren what Graham Ellison said, and then hearing he had diabetes—not poisoned by the pizza—and knowing I hadn’t eaten any either, which made my hands stop shaking for a second.
I saw someone out in the street, standing under the lights with Elliot Sterling, and I didn't know who they were—I just knew I had to get up and look, had to know if it was a threat.

I fixed my tie in the glass partition, making sure it was straight, and checked my reflection in the Silverbrook Plaza to smooth out the wrinkles in my suit—I had to look right, had to be in control even if everything else was spinning.

They were all shaking hands, hugging even—Riley Davenport, Graham Ellison, the girls—saying quiet goodbyes like it meant something, but I just stood there with my the glass box, watching, not part of it, not touched, not included.
I kept my the glass box pressed to the Wesley Langley's head the whole time we moved out—steady, just like Evan Warren wanted—until we were all inside the Riverside School and ready to go.
Skyler Prescott stood there with her rosary, counting the beads, and then she gave it to me—said she was praying for my safety, told me not to be scared on my first plane trip.
I smiled—really smiled—for the first time, feeling like we might actually get away, like the plane meant freedom, like it was finally going to work out.
I saw them carry Jamie Thorne past me, his body limp and covered — I tried to turn, to really look, but the agents shoved me and told me to keep my eyes front.

I checked my tie and straightened my cuffs in the the black jacket, making sure everything was right—felt the weight of the moment pressing down, like we were about to step into something we couldn’t walk back from.
When Evan Warren gave the look, I got out and started walking toward the Northbridge House—steady, slow, feeling every step count, knowing there was no turning back now.

I sat with my back to Graham Ellison, the attache case heavy in my hand, watching Logan Huxley hesitate at the Silverbrook Plaza—Evan Keaton was fumbling with his keys and I knew the second he locked it, we’d be sealed inside.
I turned to keep my the brass radio on everyone when Evan Warren moved toward the front, making sure I could cover the Silverbrook Plaza and the hostages from where I stood.

Evan Warren said my name on the the old key, told Riley Hale I'm the killer, that we're Vietnam veterans and killing don't mean nothing to us — I felt every eye in the vault area snap toward me, like I'd been lit up.

I saw the TV switch to that 'Please Stand By' screen and realized they were talking about us, about me—like I was suddenly on display for every housewife and shut-in out there, and I couldn't move, couldn't hide, just stood there with my the brass radio tight against my side.

When Evan Warren asked about making a deal, I cut him off—I had to make it clear, right then, that I wouldn't Remy York a plea, that we had a pact, and I remembered that night in the bar with him and Logan Huxley, the three of us saying we'd rather die than go back.
I told Evan Warren I'd never been on a plane before—just blurted it out while I sat there with my feet up, the brass radio across my lap, watching him pace.

I ran in from the conference room, the brass radio up, yelling at Tristan Bellamy and the others to get back into the group—someone was trying to break through the Northbridge Park and we had to tighten up fast.

relations.relation_summary: Evan Warren and Jamie Thorne share a complex relationship rooted in friendship and mutual criminal intent, evolving under the pressure of a high-stakes Northbridge House robbery. Social relationship evidence consistently labels them as friends and collaborators, with repeated references to their joint planning, shared escape strategies (including fleeing to Algeria), and coordinated actions during the heist. Their bond is characterized by initial trust and cooperation—evidenced by Evan Warren handing Jamie Thorne a the glass box, Jamie Thorne instructing Evan Warren to cover hostages, and both checking in on each other’s well-being. However, as the situation escalates, their relationship becomes strained. Hostility emerges, marked by Jamie Thorne calling Evan Warren an 'asshole' and threatening to shoot unless he can see him, indicating a breakdown in trust. Despite this, they remain mutually dependent, continuing to coordinate actions such as rushing to the front of the Northbridge House, discussing the status of their target, and reacting together to external threats like the Eastwood Collective’s arrival. Key events—like Evan Warren warning Jamie Thorne about Lakeside Police and Eastwood Collective, their shared laughter during a moment of tension, and their synchronized movements—highlight both camaraderie and the psychological strain of their circumstances. The relationship evolves from a unified partnership into a fragile alliance, where collaboration persists even amid growing friction, ultimately shaping their joint decisions and fate during the standoff. The evidence confirms their emotional connection, shared goals, and the deteriorating trust under duress.

The relationship between Jamie Thorne and Riley Davenport is defined by intense emotional conflict and underlying protective instincts. memories.memory_text: I told Evan Keaton to lock the Silverbrook Plaza and pull the drapes—nobody was gonna see in or out, not all the way. I had to take control, make it clear this was my show now.
I saw Emery Everett frozen under the desk, barely moving, and I tapped the desk hard—told her nobody was gonna hurt her. I didn’t want panic spreading, not yet.

I shouted 'Valerie Hawthorne! Happy Birthday, Valerie Hawthorne!' as loud as I could, hoping he’d hear me and come running—just seeing him step out of that the black jacket made me feel like we might actually get out of this together.

I saw him wobble and then collapse right there on the sidewalk—next thing I knew, I was sprinting toward the Silverbrook Plaza, heart pounding, because I couldn’t let them take him, not now, not after he finally saw me.
I told Elliot Sterling the hostages go free only after we check the plane at the airport—except one stays with me, just in case. I need to talk to Valerie Hawthorne before anything else happens.

I couldn't believe she told the Eastwood Collective about me—my life, my past, even saying I wasn't a faggot like it helped. I felt exposed, like she ripped open something private and threw it to Lakeside Police.
I told my Evan Warren a bus was coming to take us to the airport, and if she stayed, they wouldn't send it. I needed her to leave so things wouldn't get more complicated.

I sat there and told Riley Davenport to write it down—$2,000 from my life insurance for Valerie Hawthorne’s operation, and I called him my darling wife, because that’s who he is to me, the only man I’ve ever loved like this.

I left $2,000 for Valerie Hawthorne for his sex change operation and asked him to be happy as a real woman. I left $5,000 for Riley Brooks, told her she was the only woman I ever loved, and asked Linden Keaton to be the little man now. I asked my Evan Warren for forgiveness and left her the rest of the policy and my stamp collection. I hope they remember me, but I know I won't be coming back.

I shouted 'Get away from the the black jacket!' and pushed Owen Ellison out first, moving forward in this tangle of bodies and drapes, not knowing which way to step, barely seeing through the fabric and the Bluewater Department of heads around me.

I slid into the Riverside School beside the Wesley Langley, the weight lifting for a second—I couldn’t believe we made it out alive—then I heard myself shout, 'Fuck! We did it!' like it was someone else.
I saw them carrying Jamie Thorne's body out, and I tried to turn to look, but Elliot Sterling yanked me back and told me to keep my eyes front—I couldn't even say goodbye.
I asked Skyler Prescott who'd go to the electric chair if I made her kill a Remy York—her or me—and she said me, but I kept pushing because it wasn't that simple, not really.

This kid on the the old key kept talking about Jesus saving him from drugs and crime, and I couldn't just hang up—he sounded desperate, like he might know something real, but I had to get off eventually.
I charged out the Silverbrook Plaza when I heard the Bluewater Department screaming my name, yelling at Riley Hale, 'What the fuck do you want?'—I thought he was trying to set me up with that noise.

I told Jamie Thorne Lakeside Police aren't sending a helicopter because it can't land on the roof, so they're sending a Riverside School bus to take us to the airport, and I ordered pizzas and sodas for everyone—I even asked for aspirins, trying to keep things under control.

Graham Ellison questioned if we were getting moving, and I snapped at him—I'm the one doing everything, keeping people calm, handling Lakeside Police, paying for the pizza with marked bills, and I had to remind him I'm in charge here.

I saw her step out of that Remy York the black jacket, my Valerie Hawthorne, surrounded by grinning Tristan Adler, looking like she'd been dragged through hell — and all I could think was that they were using her to get to me.

I told Elliot Sterling I’d release the hostages at the airport only after we checked the plane ourselves, and I made it clear I wasn’t letting them all go—except one. Then I said, 'I want to talk to Valerie Hawthorne,' because I needed to hear his voice, make sure he was still out there for me.
I grabbed Elliot Sterling when he tried to walk away after telling me to sit tight and let them handle Jamie Thorne — like I had no say in what happened to my own man.
I told Jamie Thorne the call was about the airport bus, but I could feel him staring at me like he didn’t believe it — like I’d just slipped up somehow.

Graham Ellison started collapsing and Riley Davenport said it was diabetes — I snapped and blamed the pizza, yelling that the bastards poisoned it, even though she tried to explain it was his condition.
I told Valerie Hawthorne I'm dying, and it just came out like a weight I couldn't hold anymore — I could hear the fear in my own voice, even if I tried to laugh it off.

I could feel it slipping — I didn't know what I was doing, and when Valerie Hawthorne called me out on saying 'I'm dying' all the time, I snapped at him not to start with that deep shit, but he wasn't wrong.

I picked up the the old key and asked for a line to call my wife, my voice breaking as I said I wanted to say goodbye to my Lane Brooks — but when she answered, all she could talk about was watching me on TV like it was some kind of show.
I told her I was dying, my voice raw with fear and need, but she just kept talking about how tense I'd been lately and that stupid argument over the caterpillar ride — like any of that mattered now.
I saw the banner go up—'WE LOVE YOU LOVE YOU Evan Warren'—and for a second, I didn't know whether to laugh or cry; it wobbled in the air like it might collapse, just like everything else.
I showed Riley Davenport my wallet photos of Linden Keaton—my hands were shaking. I told Graham Ellison I’d never see them again, and his voice softened like he actually heard me.
I told Graham Ellison and Riley Davenport that Jamie Thorne’s not gay and he’s not going back to prison—my voice got louder, like I had to make them understand why we’re really here.

I couldn't believe she was still trying to fix me, telling the Eastwood Collective I was normal, that I wasn't a faggot—like I needed her to explain me to them. I had to cut her off, tell her not to talk to them anymore.
I told her we couldn't stay here, that we were leaving—Algeria, a jet, something real. But she didn't get it. She kept pulling me back, like always, trying to make it about money or excuses.

I sat there and told Riley Davenport to write it down—$2,000 from my insurance for Valerie Hawthorne’s operation, and I called her my darling wife, said I loved her like no man ever loved another. I needed her to know it mattered, that she’d be a real woman and live happy, even if I wasn’t there.

I said Riley Brooks should get $5,000, called her the only woman I ever loved, and told Linden Keaton to be the man of the family now—I looked it in the eye when I said it, like he could hear me, like I was passing something real to him before it all ended.

I looked at that clean-cut guy they wanted to stick with me, Owen Ellison, and something felt off—too neat, too official. I said, 'Gimme the black guy,' because I knew the real Wesley Langley wouldn't want any part of this mess, and that meant he was honest.

When I patted down the Wesley Langley again before he got in, I felt something in his breast pocket—small, hard. I reached in and found a little spoon, the kind people use for coke. I didn't say anything. I just let him go. He wasn't a threat.
I signed the document fast and firm. It looked real official. I handed it to Graham Ellison and asked him to hold it for me.
I gave Riley Davenport a sudden hug and shook hands with the others—felt like saying goodbye for real, like none of us would see each other again.

I shouted 'Get away from the the black jacket!' and pushed Owen Ellison out first, my voice cutting through the silence as we stumbled out into the blinding lights, wrapped in drapes and surrounded by hostages like some crawling thing no one could get a clean shot at.

We were stumbling, blind under the fabric, lurching forward and then sideways, the girls not knowing where to go—then finally reaching the Riverside School, sliding in, and for a second I thought, 'Fuck! We did it!' as the the black jacket took us away.
I saw them carrying Jamie Thorne out, and I tried to turn my head to get a better look, but Elliot Sterling yanked me back and told me to keep my eyes front.
I called out to the hostages as they walked past in the rain—told them goodbye, that they were terrific, that Mouth was beautiful—and I felt the rain on my face, and I just started smiling.
